Every department head is immediately responsible to the city manager for the effective administration of his respective department.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-104)
134:
The administrative services department shall perform all administrative duties for the mayor and council and for the city, which are not expressly assigned to another by state law, city Charter or this Code of Ordinances.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-105)
135:
The city manager shall:
Perform the duties conferred upon him by section 3.14 of the city Charter and any other applicable sections.
Keep, or cause to be kept, true, accurate and just books of accounts of the dealings and transactions of the city, which books shall show at all times the true conditions of said city, its resources and liabilities and the disposition and use of the monies coming under the control of the city.
Keep or cause to be kept in a safe place all monies, records and accounts.
Disburse funds for the various purposes of the city only when an appropriation for such purpose has been made in the annual budget and the disbursement is authorized by the mayor and council.
Perform such other duties as the mayor and council may from time to time require.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-106)
138:
The public works department shall be responsible for the proper construction and maintenance of streets, sidewalks, parks, buildings, public utilities, other movable and immovable property of the city, and refuse collection and disposal.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-107)
139:
The public works superintendent shall:
Make regular inspections of the streets, alleys and sidewalks within the city; make a written memorandum of same; and cause all defects and obstructions to be remedied at the earliest opportunity; especially shall he carry out this duty after storms or heavy rainfall.
Ensure that all highways, streets and sidewalks of the city are maintained in a clean condition; and enforce and carry out all city ordinances and regulations concerning city streets and sidewalks.
Supervise and inspect the operations of the water, sewerage, and all other public utility systems provided by the city.
Supervise the collection and disposal of refuse accumulated within the corporate limits of the city.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-108)
142:
The police department shall be responsible for the prevention and detection of crime, the enforcement of federal and state laws and city ordinances, the apprehension of violators of such laws and ordinances, and the protection of persons and property against injury from crime.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-109)
Head of municipal law enforcement agency, O.C.G.A. § 35-1-12.
143:
Supervision of police department. The chief of police shall be the chief executive officer of the police department of the city, shall have full power and authority over the management and conduct of the department, and shall be charged with the full and complete responsibility for the successful and efficient operation of said department, subject to the general laws of the state, the Charter and this Code of Ordinances, and the administrative authority of the city manager.
Responsibility for good order, conduct of police. The chief of police shall be responsible for the lawful order of the city and the general good conduct of the officers and men of the police department.
Application of duties. It shall be the duty of the chief of police, at all times, both day and night, to preserve the public peace; to protect the rights of persons and property; to provide proper police force at fires; to protect firemen and property thereat; to suppress riots and insurrections; to disperse unlawful and dangerous crowds and assemblages which obstruct free passage on public streets, sidewalks, parks, and places; to preserve order at elections and all public meetings and assemblages within the city; to regulate the movement of vehicles in the streets; to assist in the control of animals running wild upon the streets of the city; to enforce all ordinances and regulations of the city, the state, and the United States of America; to establish systems and procedures for the preservation of evidence and reports of investigations of crimes; and to conduct an aggressive continuing program of training for the members of the police department. Such enumeration of duties shall not be deemed exclusive or exhaustive, but it shall be the duty of the chief of police to perform such other duties as may from time to time be assigned to him by the appropriate authority.
Disciplinary powers. The chief of police shall have the power to suspend, with or without pay, discharge, or reduce in rank, any police officer, where such action is deemed necessary or appropriate for the preservation of the good order of the police department, the promotion of discipline and compliance with the police regulations, and the promotion of the efficient enforcement of the ordinances of the city. (Note. All employees are due appeal rights under the city personnel polices.)
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-110)
144:
The police chief shall prepare all regulations for the performance of the city police department. Regulations shall then be reviewed by the city manager and presented to the city council along with any comments that the city manager may have. Upon adoption by the mayor and council, said regulations shall become effective.
(Comp. Ords. 2005, § 3-111)

149:
Title. This division shall be known and may be cited as the "Procurement and Contract Management Ordinance."
Purpose. The purpose of this division is to: Establish consistent, transparent, and efficient procedures for all purchasing and contracting activity of the City of Dallas; Define authority, accountability, and approval requirements for procurement transactions; Ensure compliance with the City Charter, O.C.G.A. Title 36, Chapter 91, and all other applicable state and federal laws; Promote fair and open competition to obtain best value for taxpayers; and Provide for proper fiscal controls, legal review, and oversight of public expenditures.
Scope. This division applies to all city departments, officers, employees, boards, commissions, authorities, and other entities involved in the expenditure of city funds, regardless of funding source.
Exemptions. This division does not apply to: Employment contracts for city employees, which are governed by personnel policies; Contracts for legal services retained by the city attorney, which are governed by Charter section 3.15; or General obligation bonds, revenue bonds, notes, or other debt instruments issued pursuant to Charter sections 6.18 through 6.20 and applicable state law, which are not procurement transactions. Financing arrangements, lease-purchase agreements, installment contracts, and equipment financing agreements for the acquisition of goods, services, or equipment are not exempt from this Division and are governed by section 2-221.2.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § II, 6-1-2026)
150:
City manager as chief procurement officer. The city manager shall serve as the chief procurement officer of the city and shall have final approval authority for all purchases and contracts, subject to city council approval as required by this division and applicable law. The city manager's approval authority includes but is not limited to: Final determination of procurement method and solicitation type; Approval of vendor selection and award recommendations; Execution of contracts and purchase orders on behalf of the city; Resolution of vendor protests and disputes; Suspension and debarment of vendors; and Interpretation and enforcement of procurement procedures.
Procurement officer. The city manager may designate a procurement officer, typically within the finance department, to perform daily administrative functions including solicitation preparation, bid management, vendor coordination, and procurement file maintenance. Designation of a procurement officer does not diminish the city manager's final authority over all procurement decisions.
No binding obligation without city manager approval. No purchase, contract, or other obligation shall be binding upon the city unless (i) approved by a department head within the department head's delegated authority under section 2-221(a) and issued by purchase order through the finance director, or (ii) approved in writing by the city manager for purchases exceeding department head authority, and in either case reviewed and concurred in by the city attorney and finance director as required by this division. Unauthorized purchases may be declared void and shall not be honored or paid except as provided in section 2-228(b).
Electronic file management. The procurement officer shall establish and maintain an electronic file management system for all procurement records, including but not limited to requisitions, solicitations, quotations, bids, proposals, evaluations, contracts, purchase orders, change orders, and vendor correspondence. Records shall be retained in accordance with section 2-227(a).
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § II, 6-1-2026)
151:
City attorney review required. The city attorney shall review and provide written concurrence or comments prior to execution for: All written contracts regardless of dollar amount; All purchase orders exceeding $20,000.00; Any purchase order or contract containing indemnification, hold harmless, insurance, bonding, warranty, or liability provisions regardless of dollar amount; Any solicitation document, including invitations for bids, requests for proposals, and requests for qualifications, when directed by the city manager or when the anticipated contract value exceeds $50,000.00; Any modification, amendment, or change order to a previously-reviewed contract or purchase order; and Any other procurement transaction at the direction of the city manager.
Exemption for routine purchase orders. Standard purchase orders for routine goods and services under $20,000.00 using approved city forms are exempt from city attorney review provided they do not contain risk-transfer provisions described in subsection (a)(3).
Finance director certification required. The finance director shall certify in writing, prior to solicitation or award, that: Adequate funds are legally available and properly appropriated in the identified budget account for the purchase or contract; The expenditure is consistent with the budget purpose and any restrictions on the funding source; and An encumbrance has been assigned reserving the funds.
Written concurrence in procurement file. Written concurrence from the city attorney and certification from the finance director shall be filed in the procurement record prior to execution of any contract or purchase order requiring such review under this section.
Effect of legal or financial objection. If the city attorney or finance director identifies legal deficiencies, fiscal irregularities, or non-compliance with applicable law or policy, the city manager shall not proceed with the procurement until the deficiencies are resolved or the city manager provides written justification overriding the objection, which shall be retained in the procurement file.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-220, 6-1-2026)
152:
Department head authority (up to $10,000.00). Department heads may approve purchase requisitions up to $10,000.00 within their approved departmental budgets. The finance director shall issue purchase orders for approved requisitions upon verification of budget availability. The city manager retains authority to review and reverse any departmental purchase decision.
Informal quotations ($10,001.00 to $49,999.00). Purchases or contracts with an estimated value from $10,001.00 to $49,999.00 require: At least three written or electronic quotations obtained by the procurement officer using uniform specifications and terms; and Award by the city manager to the lowest responsive and responsible quotation, or to another quotation based on best value with written justification, following finance director certification and city attorney review as required by section 2-220.
Formal sealed bids or proposals ($50,000.00 and above). Purchases or contracts with an estimated value of $50,000.00 or more require: A formal sealed bid process using an invitation for bids, or a competitive proposal process using a request for proposals, as determined by the city manager based on whether price alone is the determining factor; Public advertisement in accordance with applicable law; For invitations for bids, public opening of sealed bids at the advertised date, time, and location; for requests for proposals, receipt of proposals by the deadline stated in the solicitation documents, with public disclosure of proposal scores and rankings following final award or cancellation of the solicitation, consistent with section 2-227(d) and the Georgia Open Records Act; and Award as follows: For purchases or contracts with an estimated value of $50,000.00 to $99,999.00, award shall be made by the city manager following written concurrence from the city attorney and finance director; and For purchases or contracts with an estimated value of $100,000.00 or more, or for any multi-year contract subject to subsection (d) below, award shall require prior city council approval as provided in subsection (d) of this section, in addition to written concurrence from the city attorney and finance director.
City council approval required ($100,000.00 or more; multi-year contracts). In addition to the competitive procurement requirements of subsection (c) of this section, which apply to all purchases and contracts of $50,000.00 or more regardless of the approval authority required for award, the following purchases and contracts shall require approval by the mayor and city council prior to award: Any purchase or contract with an annual value of $100,000.00 or more; Any contract exceeding one fiscal year in duration, including all renewal options and extensions, regardless of annual value; provided, however, that contracts with an aggregate total value under $25,000.00 and a duration under 36 months are excluded from this multi-year requirement; Any other contract designated by the city manager or city council as requiring council approval due to policy significance, public interest, or unusual risk profile; and Financing arrangements are subject to the provisions of section 2-221.2 and require budget adjustments as specified in the procurement procedures manual.
Professional and construction services. Notwithstanding the thresholds in subsections (a) through (d), professional services and construction contracts are subject to additional requirements as set forth in section 2-223.
Cooperative purchasing agreements. The city manager may utilize cooperative purchasing agreements as authorized in section 2-226(c), which satisfy competitive procurement requirements but remain subject to the dollar thresholds in subsection (d) of this section for council approval.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-221, 6-1-2026)
153:
Contract requirement. Formal written contracts reviewed by the city attorney and executed by the city manager are required for: All purchases of goods or services valued at $50,000.00 or more; All construction contracts regardless of amount; All professional services contracts regardless of amount; All contracts exceeding one fiscal year in duration regardless of amount; Any purchase involving performance obligations beyond simple delivery of goods or provision of routine services; and Any purchase requiring insurance, bonding, indemnification, warranty, or other risk-allocation provisions.
Purchase orders for routine purchases. Purchases not meeting the criteria in subsection (a) may be executed by purchase order on forms approved by the city manager. Purchase orders for amounts exceeding $20,000.00 shall be reviewed by the city attorney as provided in section 2-220(a)(2).
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-221.1, 6-1-2026)
154:
Authorization. The city manager is authorized to enter into financing arrangements, including but not limited to lease-purchase agreements, installment contracts, and equipment financing agreements, subject to the approval thresholds and competitive procurement requirements established in this division.
Budget adjustment requirement. All financing arrangements shall require corresponding budget adjustments to prevent duplicate appropriations for the same equipment, goods, or services. Such adjustments shall be implemented in accordance with procedures established in the procurement procedures manual.
Annual payment budgeting. Annual payments under financing arrangements shall be budgeted as operating expenses in the appropriate department budget for each fiscal year in which payments are due.
Reporting to council. The city manager shall report all financing arrangements and associated budget adjustments to the mayor and city council at the next regular meeting following execution of such arrangements.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-221.2, 6-1-2026)
155:
Authority. The city manager may authorize an emergency purchase when an unforeseen condition or circumstance requires immediate action to protect public health, safety, welfare, or city property, and when delay occasioned by competitive procurement procedures would cause serious injury to persons or property or substantial loss of essential city services.
Competition where practicable. In authorizing emergency purchases, the city manager shall make reasonable efforts to obtain competition and achieve fair pricing, considering the exigent circumstances. Competition may include obtaining telephone or electronic quotations, consulting recent procurement records, or negotiating with available vendors.
Emergency certification. For emergency purchases exceeding $20,000.00, the city manager shall execute a written emergency certification within 48 hours of authorization. The certification shall state: The specific facts and circumstances constituting the emergency; Why delay would result in serious injury or loss; Efforts made to obtain competition under the circumstances; The vendor selected and basis for selection; The total cost incurred or committed; and The expected duration of the emergency condition.
Review and reporting. Emergency certifications shall be reviewed by the finance director and city attorney for legal sufficiency. A report of all emergency purchases exceeding $20,000.00, including the emergency certification and concurrence memoranda, shall be submitted to the mayor and council at their next regular meeting following the purchase. Certifications found deficient after the fact shall be referred to the city's audit committee or external auditor for review and recommendation.
Abuse of emergency authority. Emergency purchasing authority shall not be used to circumvent competitive procurement requirements, to avoid city council approval thresholds, or to justify poor planning or lack of advance requisition. Repeated use of emergency purchasing for similar or recurring needs may be evidence of abuse and subject the responsible employee to disciplinary action.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-221.2, 6-1-2026)
156:
Qualifications—Based selection for professional services. Professional services, including but not limited to architecture, engineering, land surveying, landscape architecture, construction management (when functioning as owner's representative), planning, consulting, and other services requiring specialized professional licensure or expertise (excluding legal services retained by the city attorney, which are exempt under section 2-218(d)(2)), shall be procured using qualifications-based selection procedures consistent with O.C.G.A. § 50-22-6 and the federal Brooks Act, 40 U.S.C. §§ 1101–1104, when applicable.
Prohibition on price as selection factor. Price, fees, or cost proposals shall not be requested in the initial solicitation or used as an evaluation or selection factor for professional services covered by subsection (a). After ranking the most qualified firms, the city manager may negotiate scope and fee with the highest-ranked firm. If negotiations fail to produce a fair and reasonable agreement, the city manager shall terminate negotiations and commence negotiations with the next-ranked firm.
Construction contracts—Competitive bidding required. Construction contracts, including building construction, renovation, repair, alteration, and public works projects exceeding $250,000.00, shall comply with the competitive bidding requirements of O.C.G.A. Title 36, Chapter 91, as amended by HB 137 (2025). At a minimum: Bid advertisements shall be published at least once in a newspaper of general circulation in Paulding County at least ten calendar days before the bid opening, as required by O.C.G.A. § 36-91-50(b). The city shall target 14 calendar days as standard practice to maximize competition. Performance bonds and payment bonds shall be required for all construction contracts exceeding $250,000.00 as mandated by O.C.G.A. §§ 36-91-70 and 36-91-90, as amended, and O.C.G.A. § 13-10-1 et seq. (Little Miller Act), as amended by HB 137 (2025), in the amount of 100 percent of the contract price. Bids shall be sealed, publicly opened, and tabulated. Award shall be made to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder unless the city manager determines rejection of all bids is in the public interest, in which case written justification shall be prepared. For construction contracts requiring city council approval under section 2-221(d), the city manager's recommendation for award shall be presented to the mayor and city council for approval prior to contract execution.
Construction contracts between $100,000.00 and $250,000.00. Construction contracts with an estimated value between $100,000.00 and $249,999.00 are exempt from the formal competitive bidding requirements of O.C.G.A. Title 36, Chapter 91 pursuant to HB 137 (2025), but remain subject to the following requirements: City council approval is required for all construction contracts exceeding $100,000.00 per section 2-221(d); Competitive procurement shall be conducted using the formal sealed bid or competitive proposal procedures of section 2-221(c), as determined by the city manager based on project complexity and scope. Informal quotations under section 2-221(b) are not available for construction contracts exceeding $49,999.00; Performance and payment bonds are optional but may be required by the city manager when warranted by contractor experience, project risk, substantial subcontractor participation, or other relevant factors. The determination to require bonds shall be documented in the procurement file with written justification; All other provisions of this division apply, including legal and finance review requirements, formal written contract requirements, and ethical standards.
Federal requirements. When federal funds are used for professional services or construction, additional federal procurement requirements shall apply as set forth in section 2-224.
Design-build and construction manager at risk. Alternative project delivery methods such as design-build or construction manager at risk may be used when authorized by state law and when the city manager determines such methods serve the public interest. Procurement procedures for alternative delivery methods shall comply with applicable state statutes and shall be established in the procurement procedures manual.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-223, 6-1-2026)
157:
Applicability. When any portion of a procurement is funded by federal grants, cooperative agreements, reimbursement programs, or other federal financial assistance, the procurement shall comply with all applicable federal statutes, regulations, and funding conditions in addition to the requirements of this division and state law.
Identification and incorporation of requirements. Upon determination that federal funds are involved, the department initiating the procurement shall immediately notify the city attorney and finance director. The city attorney shall identify applicable federal requirements, which may include but are not limited to: Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards (2 C.F.R. Part 200); Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements for construction (40 U.S.C. § 3141 et seq.); Buy America or Buy American preferences; Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) or other small business participation goals; Federal suspension and debarment verification (2 C.F.R. Part 180); Procurement method restrictions specific to the funding program; Cost or price analysis requirements; and Federal funding agency-specific terms and conditions.
Solicitation documents. The procurement officer shall incorporate all applicable federal requirements into solicitation documents, including required certifications, representations, compliance obligations, contract clauses, and flow-down provisions to subcontractors.
Conflict resolution. In the event of a conflict between city procedures and federal requirements, federal requirements shall control to the extent necessary to maintain eligibility for federal funding. The city attorney shall document any such conflict and the resolution in the procurement file.
Federal Highway Administration projects. Procurement of engineering and design-related services for projects funded by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) under Title 23, U.S.C., shall comply with the qualifications-based selection requirements of 23 U.S.C. § 112(b)(2) and 23 C.F.R. Part 172, in addition to the Brooks Act provisions of subsection 2-223(a). Detailed procedures for FHWA-funded procurements shall be set forth in the procurement procedures manual or in project-specific procurement compliance guidance issued by the city attorney in consultation with the city manager.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, 6-1-2026)
158:
Prohibition on financial interest. No city officer, elected official, or employee who participates in or has responsibility for any aspect of a procurement transaction shall have a direct or indirect financial interest in any vendor, contractor, or consultant seeking to contract with the city. For purposes of this subsection, participation includes but is not limited to specification preparation, requisition approval, vendor selection, evaluation, contract negotiation, contract administration, or payment authorization.
Prohibition on gratuities. No city officer, elected official, or employee involved in procurement shall solicit or accept, directly or indirectly, any gift, gratuity, favor, entertainment, loan, or other thing of value from any vendor, contractor, consultant, or other person seeking to do business with the city, except as may be permitted by the city's ethics ordinance or state law for items of de minimis value.
Vendor conflict disclosure. All vendors submitting bids, proposals, or quotations to the city shall file a written conflict-of-interest disclosure statement, disclosing any business or financial relationship between the vendor, its principals, or its subcontractors and any city official or employee. The disclosure shall be required by solicitation documents consistent with O.C.G.A. § 36-35-3(a), and, for public works solicitations, O.C.G.A. § 36-91-21(b)(4) and O.C.G.A. § 36-91-21(c)(1)(A) and (C). The disclosure shall be filed with the bid or proposal and updated promptly if circumstances change during contract performance. Failure to disclose a known conflict shall constitute grounds for bid or proposal disqualification and may result in contract termination and debarment.
Violations and penalties. Violations of this section by city personnel may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment. Violations by vendors may result in disqualification of the bid or proposal, contract termination, and debarment from city contracts for a period of up to three years. Nothing in this section limits criminal prosecution under O.C.G.A. § 16-10-2 or other applicable law.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, § 2-225, 6-1-2026)
159:
Surplus property designation. The city manager, with concurrence from the finance director, may declare city-owned personal property surplus when it is obsolete, no longer needed for city operations, uneconomical to maintain, or otherwise appropriate for disposal. Real property may only be declared surplus and disposed of in accordance with the procedures established in the City Charter and applicable state law.
Disposal methods. Surplus personal property may be sold, traded, donated to governmental or nonprofit entities, or disposed of by any lawful means authorized by O.C.G.A. § 36-37-6. Surplus items with an estimated fair market value exceeding $500.00 shall be sold by sealed bid, public auction, or online auction following public notice of at least ten calendar days.
Cooperative purchasing authority. The city may participate in state, regional, or national cooperative purchasing programs authorized by O.C.G.A. §§ 50-5-100 through 50-5-103, O.C.G.A. § 50-5-51(9), and O.C.G.A. § 36-34-2. The city manager may execute cooperative purchasing agreements and intergovernmental agreements for joint procurement, provided the city's maximum annual financial commitment under the agreement does not exceed $100,000.00. Cooperative agreements exceeding this threshold require city council approval by resolution. Cooperative purchasing agreements with a duration exceeding one fiscal year are subject to the multi-year contract approval requirements of section 2-221(d)(2) regardless of the annual commitment amount.
Effect of cooperative purchasing. Individual purchases made through an approved cooperative purchasing agreement or state contract satisfy the competitive procurement requirements of this division, but remain subject to the dollar thresholds in section 2-221(d) for city council approval. Purchases through cooperative agreements shall comply with the legal review, financial certification, and contract execution requirements of this division.
Compliance with cooperative program requirements. When utilizing cooperative purchasing agreements, state contracts, or federal procurement programs (including but not limited to the Georgia 1122 Program, Georgia state contracts, GSA federal supply schedules, or other authorized cooperative purchasing programs), the city shall strictly comply with all eligibility requirements, terms and conditions, purchasing procedures, and restrictions imposed by the administering agency or sponsoring entity. The procurement officer shall verify the city's eligibility, obtain any required registrations or authorizations, and ensure that goods or services sought are within the scope of the applicable cooperative agreement or state contract. Documentation of compliance with cooperative program requirements shall be maintained in the procurement file. Individual purchases through cooperative agreements remain subject to city manager approval and city council thresholds established in section 2-221(d).
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, 6-1-2026)
160:
Records retention. Procurement records, including but not limited to requisitions, solicitations, quotations, bids, proposals, evaluations, tabulations, contracts, purchase orders, change orders, payment records, and correspondence, shall be retained in accordance with the records retention schedule for Georgia local governments published by the Georgia Archives, but in no event less than five years from the date of final payment or contract completion, whichever occurs later.Extended retention periods apply as follows: Construction contracts. Seven years from final payment; Federal or grant-funded contracts. Three years after submission of the final federal financial report or as specified in the grant agreement, whichever is longer, or as otherwise required by 2 C.F.R. § 200.334; and Contracts involving ongoing warranty, maintenance obligations, or potential liability exposure. Until all obligations and exposures terminate, plus five years.
Annual procurement report. The city manager shall provide an annual procurement summary report to the mayor and council no later than 90 days after the close of each fiscal year. The report shall include: Total number of contracts and purchase orders executed during the fiscal year; Total dollar value of contracts and purchase orders by category (construction, professional services, goods, other services); Number and type of procurements by method (quotations, sealed bids, proposals, sole source, emergency); Average procurement processing times; Summary of emergency purchases; Summary of vendor protests and resolutions; Identification of any significant compliance issues or recommendations for process improvement.
Audit review. The city's annual independent financial audit conducted pursuant to Charter section 6.25 shall include a review of procurement compliance, including testing of competitive procurement procedures, approval requirements, contract execution, and adherence to applicable laws and policies. Audit findings related to procurement shall be reported to the city council with management's response and corrective action plan.
Public access to records. Public access to procurement records shall be governed by the Georgia Open Records Act, O.C.G.A. § 50-18-70 et seq. During active solicitation periods (from issuance of solicitation documents until final award or cancellation), the City may withhold disclosure of unopened bids or proposals, evaluation materials, internal deliberations, vendor scoring or ranking, and pre-decisional memoranda to protect the integrity of the competitive process and prevent disclosure of confidential vendor information. After award or cancellation, all procurement records are subject to Open Records Act disclosure except as exempted by state law.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, 6-1-2026)
161:
Employee violations. Any city employee who authorizes, approves, executes, or incurs a financial obligation on behalf of the city contrary to the requirements of this division or the procurement procedures manual shall be subject to disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment. Supervisors and department heads are responsible for ensuring subordinates comply with this division.
Unauthorized purchases. Purchases or contracts made in violation of this division are not binding on the city and may be declared void by the city manager. Unauthorized purchases shall not be honored or paid by the city except as follows: If goods have been received or services rendered, the city manager may, with written justification, ratify the purchase to avoid unjust enrichment or to mitigate damages to the city; or If ratification is denied, the employee responsible for the unauthorized purchase may be held personally liable for the cost.
Vendor violations. Vendors that violate city or state procurement laws, regulations, or contract terms may be subject to: Disqualification of bids or proposals; Termination of existing contracts for default; Withholding of payment for non-compliant performance; Debarment or suspension from city contracts for a period of up to three years; and Pursuit of any other legal or equitable remedies available to the city, including but not limited to monetary damages, specific performance, or injunctive relief.
Referral for investigation. When violations of this division involve potential fraud, theft, embezzlement, misappropriation of public funds, or other criminal conduct, the city manager shall refer the matter to the appropriate law enforcement agency for investigation and shall notify the mayor, city council, and city attorney.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, 6-1-2026)
162:
Adoption and maintenance. The city manager shall adopt and maintain a procurement procedures manual establishing detailed administrative procedures, timelines, forms, documentation requirements, and operational standards governing all procurement activity of the city. The manual shall be consistent with this division, the City Charter, and applicable state and federal law.
Content. The procurement procedures manual shall address, at minimum: Requisition submission and review processes; Budget verification and encumbrance procedures; Vendor solicitation methods for quotations, sealed bids, and competitive proposals; Evaluation criteria, scoring methods, and committee procedures; Responsiveness and responsibility standards for vendor qualification; Contract negotiation and execution procedures; Insurance, bonding, and surety requirements; Change order and contract amendment procedures and approval limits; Single-source and sole-source justification requirements; Vendor performance monitoring and documentation; Suspension, debarment, and protest procedures; Federal procurement compliance procedures when applicable; Forms, templates, and checklists for procurement activities; and Any other procedures necessary for efficient, compliant, and transparent procurement operations.
Administrative amendment authority. The city manager may amend the procurement procedures manual administratively without city council action. Amendments shall be dated, assigned a version number, and published on the city's website. Material changes shall be communicated to department heads and procurement staff.
Public availability. The current procurement procedures manual, including all amendments, shall be maintained on the city's official website and provided to all department heads. Copies shall be made available to vendors and members of the public upon request.
Binding effect. The procurement procedures manual constitutes official city policy with full regulatory effect. Compliance with the manual is mandatory for all city personnel involved in procurement activities unless the city manager grants a specific written waiver documented in the procurement file.
(Ord. No. OA-2026-03, 6-1-2026)

The following words, terms and phrases, when used in this article, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:
Board means any member of any board appointed or elected by the mayor and council of the city.
City means the City of Dallas, Georgia.
City official or official, unless otherwise expressly defined, means the mayor, members of the city council, municipal court judges (including substitute judges), city manager, assistant city managers, city clerk, deputy city clerks, whether such person is salaried, hired or elected, and all other persons holding positions designated by the city Charter, as it may be amended from time to time. The term "city official," unless otherwise expressly defined, includes individuals appointed by the mayor and city council to all city commissioners, committees, boards, task forces, or other city bodies unless specifically exempted from this article by the city council.
Commission means any member of any commission appointed or elected by the mayor and council of the city.
Council means the city council.
Decision means any ordinance, resolution, contract, franchise, formal action or other matter voted on by the city council and other city board or commission, as well as the discussions of deliberations of the council, board, or commission which can or may lead to a vote or formal action by that body.
Discretionary authority means the power to exercise any judgment in a decision or action.
Employee means any person who is a fulltime or parttime employee of the city.
Entity means a sole proprietorship, partnership, limited partnership, firm, corporation, professional corporation, holding company, joint stock company, receivership, trust or any other entity recognized by law through which business may be conducted.
Immediate family means spouse, mother, father, brother, sister, son, or daughter of any city official or employee.
Incidental interest means an interest of a city official or employee in a person, entity or property which is not a substantial interest and which has insignificant value.
Mayor means the mayor of the city.
Remote interest means an interest of a person or entity, including a city official, or employee, who would be affected in the same way as the general public. The interest of a city official or employee in the property tax rate, general city fees, city utility charges, or a comprehensive zoning ordinance or similar decisions incidental to the extent that the councilmember would be in common with the general public.
Substantial interest.
The term "substantial interest" means a known interest of a city official or employee, either directly or through a member of the immediate family, in another person or entity: The interest is ownership of five percent or more of the voting stock, shares or equity of the entity or ownership of $5,000.00 or more of the equity or market value of the entity; The funds received by the person from the other person or entity either during the previous 12 months or the previous calendar year equaled or exceeded $5,000.00 in salary, bonuses, commissions, or professional fees or $5,000.00 in payment for goods, products or nonprofessional services, or ten percent of the recipient's gross income during that period, whichever is less; The person serves as a corporate officer or member of the board of directors or other governing board of the for-profit entity other than a corporate entity owned or created by the city council; or The person is a creditor, debtor, or guarantor of the person or entity in an amount of $5,000.00 or more.
The term "substantial interest," of a city official or employee in real property, means an interest in real property, which is an equitable or legal ownership, with a market value of $5,000.00 or more.
(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.4, 4-7-2008)
187:
The public judges its government by the way public officials and employees conduct themselves in the posts to which they are elected or appointed.
All government, of right, originates with the people, is founded upon their will only, and is instituted solely for the good of the whole. Public officers are the trustees and servants of the people and are at all times amenable to them (Ga. Const. art. I, § II, ¶ I).
The people of this state have the inherent right of regulating their internal government. Government is instituted for the protection, security, and benefit of the people; and at all times they have the right to alter or reform the same whenever the public good may require it (Ga. Const. art. I, § II, ¶ II).
The people have a right to expect that every public official and employee of the city will conduct himself in a manner that will end to preserve the public confidence in and respect for the government he represents.
Such confidence and respect can be best promoted if every public official and employee of the city, whether paid or unpaid, and whether elected or appointed, will uniformly: Treat all citizens with courtesy, impartiality, fairness, and equality under the law; and Avoid conflicts between their private self-interest and the public interest.
(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.1, 4-7-2008)
188:
It is the policy of the city that the proper operation of democratic government requires that public officials and employees be independent, impartial and responsible to the people; that governmental decisions and policy be made in proper channels of the government structure; that public office and employment by the city not be used for personal gain; and that the public have confidence in the integrity of its government. In recognition of these goals, a code of ethics for all city officials and employees of the city, are hereby adopted.
This article has the following purposes: To encourage high ethical standards in official conduct by city officials and city employees; To establish guidelines for ethical standards of conduct for all such officials by setting forth those acts or actions that are incompatible with the best interest of the city; To require disclosure by such officials of private financial or other interest in matters that affect the city; and To serve as a basis for disciplining those who refuse to abide by its terms.
The provisions of this article shall not apply to political contributions, loans, expenditures, reports or regulation of political campaigns or the conduct of candidates in such campaigns.
(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.2, 4-7-2008)
189:
The provisions of this article shall be applicable to all members of the city council, city employees, planning commission, board of appeals, historic preservation commission, all advisory commissions, and committee members.
(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.3, 4-7-2008)
190:
No city official or employee shall use such position to secure special privileges or exemptions for such person or others, or to secure confidential information for any other purpose other than official responsibilities.
No city official or employee shall participate in or vote on in any matter before the council, board or commission in which he has a substantial interest, shall fail to disclose for the common good for the record such interest prior to any discussion or vote.
No city official or employee shall act as an agent or attorney for another in any matter before the city council or any board or commission.
No city official or employee shall solicit or accept directly or indirectly anything of value from any person, corporation, or group: Which has, or is seeking to obtain, contractual or other business or financial relationships with the city; Which, in exchange for the thing of value, seeks to have a city official or employee exercise a matter of discretion in his favor; Which, in exchange for the thing of value, seeks to have interest which may be affected by the performance or nonperformance of the official duty of the city official or employee. This subsection shall not apply to campaign contributions which shall be reported as required by the laws of the state.
No city official or employee shall enter into any contract with the city except as specifically authorized by state statutes. Any councilmember or member of a board or commission or employee who has a proprietary interest in an agency doing business with the city shall make known that interest in writing to the city council and the city clerk.
All public funds shall be used for the general welfare of the people and not for personal economic gain of any city official or employee.
All public property owned by the city shall be disposed of in accordance with the laws of the state.
No city official or employee shall solicit or accept other employment to be performed or compensation to be received while still a city official or employee, if the employment or compensation could reasonably be expected to impair judgment or performances of city duties.
If a city official or employee accepts or is soliciting a promise of future employment from any person or entity who has a substantial interest in a person, entity or property which would be affected by any decision upon which the official or employee might reasonably be expected to act, investigate, advise, or make a recommendation, the official or employee shall disclose the fact to the board or commission on which he serves or to his supervisor and shall take no further action on matters regarding the potential future employer.
No city official or employee shall use city facilities, personnel, equipment or supplies for private purposes, except to the extent such are lawfully available to the public.
No city official or employee shall grant or make available to any person any consideration, treatment, advantage or favor beyond that which is the general practice to grant or make available to the public at large.
A city official or employee shall not use government property of any kind for other than officially approved activities, nor shall he direct employees to use such property for the purposes.
Meetings of the council shall be conducted in accordance with the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, title 50, chapter 14, as amended, and title 36, chapter 80, section 1, as amended, as it applies to municipalities.

(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.6, 4-7-2008)

(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.7, 4-7-2008)
193:
Any persons violating any provisions of this policy are subject to: Written and oral reprimand by majority vote of the mayor and council of the city; or Request for resignation by majority vote of the mayor and council of the city.

(Ord. No. 2008-05, § 3-601.9, 4-7-2008)

City officials or employees shall not accept any gifts, loans, rewards, favors, or services that may reasonably tend to improperly influence them in the discharge of their official duties. City employment shall be considered to be the primary employment of all fulltime employees. No fulltime employee may engage in outside employment which will interfere with the interest of city service. Standards by which some employment is not acceptable include, but are not limited to: Illegal activity; Employment that, by virtue of association, will adversely reflect upon the reputation of the city; High hazard or fatiguing work which might detract from or reduce the employee's ability to perform any activity within the scope of the employee's work or duties required by the city.

196:
Ethics committee. The ethics committee shall consist of three persons, one appointed by the mayor, one appointed by the council, and the third appointed by the two above named, subject to approval by a majority vote of the mayor and city council. The third member of the ethics committee shall be a member in good standing of the state bar. All members shall be residents of the city, and shall serve a two-year term. All vacancies of this ethics committee shall be filled by majority vote of the mayor and council.
Receipt of complaints. All complaints against city officials or employees shall be filed with the ethics committee. The ethics committee may require that oral complaints, and complaints illegibly or informally drawn, be reduced to a written complaint on such form as may be prescribed by the mayor and council. Upon receipt of a complaint in proper form, the ethics committee shall review it to determine whether the complaint is unjustified, frivolous, patently unfounded, or fails to state facts sufficient to invoke the disciplinary jurisdiction of the mayor and council. The ethics committee shall be empowered to collect evidence and information concerning any complaint and to add the findings and results of its investigations to the file containing such complaint. All files shall be maintained by the city clerk. Upon completion of its investigation of a complaint, the ethics committee shall be empowered to dismiss those complaints which are unjustified, frivolous, patently unfounded, or which fail to state facts sufficient to invoke the disciplinary jurisdiction of the city council; provided, however, that a rejection of such a complaint by the ethics committee shall not deprive the complaining party of any action he might otherwise have as prescribed by law against the respondent government servant. The ethics committee shall be empowered to conduct probable cause investigations, to take evidence and hold hearings where provided for in the rules. The mayor and council shall adopt all forms for formal complaints, subpoenas, notices, applications for reinstatement and any other written instruments necessary or desirable under these rules. The ethics committee shall report to the mayor and council all complaints which require any disciplinary action. The mayor and council shall set a time, date and place for any required hearing on any disciplinary action with not less than 15 days prior written notice of any such hearing to any affected city official or employee, board member, or committee member. The following words, terms and phrases, when used in this article, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:

205:
The city is a creditor pursuant to 16 CFR 681.2 due to its provision or maintenance of covered accounts for which payment is made in arrears.
Covered accounts offered to customers for the provision of city services include utilities, water, sewer, garbage, etc.
The city's previous experience with identity theft related to covered accounts is as follows: the city is aware of identity theft which has occurred in other places and to other businesses located in the county.
The processes of opening a new covered account, restoring an existing covered account and making payments on such accounts have been identified as potential processes in which identity theft could occur.
The city limits access to personal identifying information to those employees responsible for or otherwise involved in opening or restoring covered accounts or accepting payment for use of covered accounts. Information provided to such employees is entered directly into the city's computer system and is not otherwise recorded.
The city determines that there is a low to moderate risk of identity theft occurring in the following ways: Use by an applicant of another person's personal identifying information to establish a new covered account; Use of a previous customer's personal identifying information by another person in an effort to have service restored in the previous customer's name; Use of another person's credit card, bank account, or other method of payment by a customer to pay such customer's covered account or accounts; and Use by a customer desiring to restore such customer's covered account of another person's credit card, bank account, or other method of payment.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-204, 4-6-2009)
206:

Such information shall be entered directly into the city's computer system and/or other filing system and shall not otherwise be recorded.
Each account shall be assigned an account number.
Notifications from consumer reporting agencies. The city does not request, receive, obtain or maintain information about its utility customers from any consumer reporting agency.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-205, 4-6-2009)
207:
Access to customer accounts shall be password protected and shall be limited to authorized city personnel.
Such passwords shall be at least five characters in length and shall contain letters, numbers and/or symbols.
Any unauthorized access to or other breach of customer accounts is to be reported immediately to the city manager and the password changed immediately.
Personal identifying information included in customer accounts is considered confidential and any request or demand for such information shall be immediately forwarded to the city manager and the city attorney.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-206, 4-6-2009)
208:
In the event that credit card payments that are made over the Internet are processed through a third party service provider, such third party service provider shall certify that it has an adequate identity theft prevention program in place that is applicable to such payments.
All credit card payments made over the telephone or the city's website shall be entered directly into the customer's account information in the computer data base.
Account statements and receipts for covered accounts shall include only the last four digits of the credit or debit card or the bank account used for payment of the covered account.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-207, 4-6-2009)
209:
All employees responsible for or involved in the process of opening a covered account, restoring a covered account or accepting payment for a covered account shall check for red flags as indicators of possible identity theft and such red flags may include:
Alerts. Alerts from consumer reporting agencies, fraud detection agencies or service providers. Examples of alerts include, but are not limited to: A fraud or active duty alert that is included with a consumer report; A notice of credit freeze in response to a request for a consumer report; A notice of address discrepancy provided by a consumer reporting agency; Indications of a pattern of activity in a consumer report that is inconsistent with the history and usual pattern of activity of an applicant or customer, such as: A recent and significant increase in the volume of inquiries; An unusual number of recently established credit relationships; A material change in the use of credit, especially with respect to recently established credit relationships; or An account that was closed for cause or identified for abuse of account privileges by a financial institution or creditor.
Suspicious documents. Examples of suspicious documents include: Documents provided for identification that appear to be altered or forged; Identification on which the photograph or physical description is inconsistent with the appearance of the applicant or customer; Identification on which the information is inconsistent with information provided by the applicant or customer; Identification on which the information is inconsistent with readily accessible information that is on file with the financial institution or creditor, such as a signature card or a recent check; or An application that appears to have been altered or forged, or appears to have been destroyed and reassembled.
Suspicious personal identification. Suspicious personal identification, such as suspicious address change. Examples of suspicious identifying information include: Personal identifying information that is inconsistent with external information sources used by the financial institution or creditor. For example: The address does not match any address in the consumer report; or The Social Security number (SSN) has not been issued, or is listed on the Social Security Administration's death master file. Personal identifying information provided by the customer is not consistent with other personal identifying information provided by the customer, such as a lack of correlation between the SSN range and date of birth. Personal identifying information or a phone number or address is associated with known fraudulent applications or activities as indicated by internal or third-party sources used by the financial institution or creditor. Other information provided, such as fictitious mailing address, mail-drop addresses, jail addresses, invalid phone numbers, pager numbers or answering services, is associated with fraudulent activity. The SSN provided is the same as that submitted by other applicants or customers. The address or telephone number provided is the same as or similar to the account number or telephone number submitted by an unusually large number of applicants or customers. The applicant or customer fails to provide all required personal identifying information on an application or in response to notification that the application is incomplete. Personal identifying information is not consistent with personal identifying information that is on file with the financial institution or creditor. The applicant or customer cannot provide authenticating information beyond that which generally would be available from a wallet or consumer report.
Suspicious or unusual activity. Unusual use of or suspicious activity relating to a covered account. Examples of suspicious activity include: Shortly following the notice of a change of address for an account, city receives a request for the addition of authorized users on the account. A new revolving credit account is used in a manner commonly associated with known patterns of fraud patterns. For example, the customer fails to make the first payment or makes an initial payment, but no subsequent payments. An account is used in a manner that is not consistent with established patterns of activity on the account. There is, for example: Nonpayment when there is no history of late or missed payments; A material change in purchasing or spending patterns. An account that has been inactive for a long period of time is used (taking into consideration the type of account, the expected pattern of usage and other relevant factors). Mail sent to the customer is returned repeatedly as undeliverable although transactions continue to be conducted in connection with the customer's account. The city is notified that the customer is not receiving paper account statements. The city is notified of unauthorized charges or transactions in connection with a customer's account. The city is notified by a customer, law enforcement or another person that it has opened a fraudulent account for a person engaged in identity theft.
Notification of possible identity theft or phishing relating to covered accounts. Notice from customers, law enforcement, victims or other reliable sources regarding possible identity theft or phishing relating to covered accounts.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-208, 4-6-2009)
210:
In the event that any city employee responsible for or involved in restoring an existing covered account or accepting payment for a covered account becomes aware of red flags indicating possible identity theft with respect to existing covered accounts, such employee shall use his discretion to determine whether such red flag or combination of red flags suggests a threat of identity theft. If, in his discretion, such employee determines that identity theft or attempted identity theft is likely or probable, such employee shall immediately report such red flags to the clerk of the city. If, in his discretion, such employee deems that identity theft is unlikely or that reliable information is available to reconcile red flags, the employee shall convey this information to the city attorney of the city, who may, in his discretion, determine that no further action is necessary. If the city attorney, in his discretion, determines that further action is necessary, a city employee shall perform one or more of the following responses, as determined to be appropriate by the city attorney: Contact the customer; Make the following changes to the account if, after contacting the customer, it is apparent that someone other than the customer has accessed the customer's covered account: Change any account numbers, passwords, security codes, or other security devices that permit access to an account; or Close the account; Cease attempts to collect additional charges from the customer and decline to sell the customer's account to a debt collector in the event that the customer's account has been accessed without authorization and such access has caused additional charges to accrue; Notify a debt collector within 48 hours of the discovery of likely or probable identity theft relating to a customer account that has been sold to such debt collector in the event that a customer's account has been sold to a debt collector prior to the discovery of the likelihood or probability of identity theft relating to such account; Notify law enforcement, in the event that someone other than the customer has accessed the customer's account causing additional charges to accrue or accessing personal identifying information; or Take other appropriate action to prevent or mitigate identity theft.
In the event that any city employee responsible for or involved in opening a new covered account becomes aware of red flags indicating possible identity theft with respect to an application for a new account, such employee shall use his discretion to determine whether such red flag or combination of red flags suggests a threat of identity theft. If, in his discretion, such employee determines that identity theft or attempted identity theft is likely or probable, such employee shall immediately report such red flags to the city clerk. If, in his discretion, such employee deems that identity theft is unlikely or that reliable information is available to reconcile red flags, the employee shall convey this information to the city attorney, who may in his discretion determine that no further action is necessary. If the city attorney, in his discretion, determines that further action is necessary, a city employee shall perform one or more of the following responses, as determined to be appropriate by the city attorney: Request additional identifying information from the applicant; Deny the application for the new account; Notify law enforcement of possible identity theft; or Take other appropriate action to prevent or mitigate identity theft.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-209, 4-6-2009)
212:
The city clerk is responsible for oversight of the program and for program implementation. The city manager is responsible for reviewing reports prepared by staff regarding compliance with red flag requirements and with recommending material changes to the program, as necessary in the opinion of the city manager, to address changing identity theft risks and to identify new or discontinued types of covered accounts. Any recommended material changes to the program shall be submitted to the city council for consideration by the council. The city clerk will report to the city manager at least annually on compliance with the red flag requirements. The report will address material matters related to the program and evaluate issues such as: The effectiveness of the policies and procedures of city in addressing the risk of identity theft in connection with the opening of covered accounts and with respect to existing covered accounts; Service provider arrangements; Significant incidents involving identity theft and management's response; and Recommendations for material changes to the program. The city clerk is responsible for providing training to all employees responsible for or involved in opening a new covered account, restoring an existing covered account or accepting payment for a covered account with respect to the implementation and requirements of the identity theft prevention program.
The city clerk shall exercise his discretion in determining the amount and substance of training necessary.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-211, 4-6-2009)
213:
In the event that the city engages a service provider to perform an activity in connection with one or more covered accounts, the city clerk shall exercise his discretion in reviewing such arrangements in order to ensure, to the best of his ability, that the service provider's activities are conducted in accordance with policies and procedures, agreed upon by contract, that are designed to detect any red flags that may arise in the performance of the service provider's activities and take appropriate steps to prevent or mitigate identity theft.
(Ord. No. 2009-09, § 4-212, 4-6-2009)
